utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T. The Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning, all. The -- as usual may we have the appearances, please. And the Chamber has been alerted, and I suppose counsel and the parties have as well, that weather conditions at the other end of the transmission that we've been receiving may create certain technical problems, so it's something that we should anticipate the possibility of in the course of today. Yes, the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Joanna Korner and Case Manager Crispian Smith for the Prosecution, and no, we hadn't been told anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Appearing for Stanisic Defence, myself and Zecevic and Mr. Cvijetic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For Zupljanin Defence, Igor Pantelic, Dragan Krgovic, and Eric Tully. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just one thing, Your Honours, just before we carry on. We, yesterday, saw the motion which is Stanisic's request for reconsideration of Your Honours' ruling on 92 ter witnesses. We were going to suggest that it's so allied to the topic that we were going to discuss in the 65 ter that we would deal with that on an oral basis rather than responding in writing, therefore not increasing the ever-increasing load of written matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner. Speaking of the 65 ter conference, we will convene it as soon as the Prosecution has produced a list of witnesses for at least the nest 8 weeks, 10 if possible, indicating the names and the times that the Prosecution seeks to spend for the examination-in-chief. So soon as we have the list, we can then have the conference.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I didn't realise it was a precursor to the conference, but you can have that this morning, in fact before the next break as it's ready, as I said in my e-mail yesterday to the legal officers. We have got a list of all the witnesses between now and Christmas, with times estimated. And obviously subject to the usual problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, and gentlemen of the Defence, next week is going to be difficult to find time to have the 65 ter conference because we are sitting in extended sessions, so I wonder if the list is out today, whether it would make sense to have the 65 ter conference tomorrow. Is that too early for the parties? Otherwise we'll have to wait for next week again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't think it's early if we can have it tomorrow. I mean, depends whether the Prosecution can produce the list.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As I say, can I make it absolutely clear, I have no doubt that Ms. Pidwell is watching, the list is out right now. So you will get it before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Can I then the Registrar to see if we can book Room 177 for the purpose of a 65 ter meeting tomorrow at, say, 2.30 after the session. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel. We resume the hearing --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Via videolink] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: -- that was suspended yesterday. I would remind you that you are still on your oath. I believe that when we took the adjournment yesterday, counsel for the Prosecution had completed her cross-examination and Mr. Cvijetic - pardon me with the pronunciation - had begun his cross-examination. I would now invite him to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Colonel Basara, good morning.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, yesterday we broke off when we were discussing the entry and withdrawal of the Yugoslav People's Army into Bosnia and Herzegovina territory. The Prosecution showed you an order yesterday of the commander of the 5th Corps of the 1st of April. However, I concluded on the basis of your testimony that you are talking about the following order that specifically designates the tasks for your brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I would like to ask the Registry to place Defence Exhibit 1D00-4486 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Colonel, can you see on the screen -- but I also think that we sent this document to you through the authorised staff member to Belgrade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. This is a regular order in the standard form where it can be seen that the Yugoslav People's Army is leaving Croatia. Can you please look at page 3 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we also look at the page on our screens here, page 3 for the Trial Chamber. I think we have the decision on the screen. In the Serbian we also need to look at page 3, please. Can you look at the page after that, page 4, because this was a certificate by the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Basara, can you please look at item 3 where your brigade is issued the assignment, and where it states that it is your duty to protect the population and prevent inter-ethnic conflict; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Am I right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Colonel Basara, are you aware that in the period when you entered Bosnia-Herzegovina, the inter-ethnic relations were already disrupted?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The inter-ethnic relations were interrupted.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Was there a danger of escalation and of civil war?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Did the arming take place outside of the legal channels of the Yugoslav People's Army and were para-legal forces created?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, both sides began to arm themselves without any control and without this being under the command of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Colonel Basara, pursuant to the federal regulations that were still in force at the time, the Yugoslav People's Army's mandate was to disarm such units and to prevent an armed uprising and the escalation of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The units did take certain measures but did not manage to prevent this completely because it was impossible because of the political situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Colonel Basara, I actually want to talk about that topic with you a little bit. I would like to show you the next Defence document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please place it on the screen. I think you also had the opportunity to look at this document in Belgrade. This is 1D00-149C.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, you are right. I forgot -- yes, you are right, Your Honours. Can we please have the previous document admitted because that document is of the 1st of April, and this one that we are looking at now is of the 2nd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I would like you just to remind us exactly who authored this document and who signed it, and it was 1st of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. General Talic authored both documents the following day on the 2nd of April. The document is dated the 2nd of April, and it follows the document of the 1st of April that was admitted or tendered yesterday by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So it's 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but I would like to have this document admitted, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, Mr. Cvijetic, but I'm slightly confused. We haven't got a document that says 1D00149C. Is this the document that a Colonel Basara has just looked at, because if so, that's the 2nd of April.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think the number that is -- [Overlapping speakers]... the exhibit that has just been admitted is 1D18.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Korner, this is the order that Judge Harhoff has mentioned and that has been tendered. We are only now discussing the document that follows. Is that more clear now?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much, but the document you are now going to look at you say is numbered 149C; right? We don't have a 149C from you. If you just tell us what the document is, and we'll be able to find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm hopefully going to eliminate all the confusion. The definite number of the document is 1D00422. My apologies. Is it all right now? May I continue, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at the document now that we do have the correct number. We can see it in the B/C/S now, and we just need to see the English version as well. Your Honour, the document was sent to Belgrade, but the document was also received from the Secretariat of the government of Republika Srpska that is investigating events that happened during the war, and collecting evidence regarding war crimes, and they sent this document to us at our request. I would like to show it to the witness, and I would like to talk to him about the content of that document. If you permit me, I would like to begin. May I continue, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did raise this document yesterday in an e-mail with Mr. Zecevic and Mr. Pantelic, I wasn't sure whose document it was. Simply this, because there is no date, no signature, and nothing to show who prepared this document. And I hear what Mr. Cvijetic says. Can he give any further information about the providence of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, pursuant to your instructions, I would like to show this document to the witness so that he can recognise the contents and the accuracy of the contents for me in the document, and I would like to have it admitted in that way. I'm not going to suggest anything to the witness, I'm going to ask him to try to recognise who the author of this document is. I'm not going to influence things one way or the other and try to influence the witness. So if nobody has anything against that, and I think that Madam Korner is in agreement with that, then I will continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Basara, or Colonel Basara, do you have this document in front of you which is named the Chronology of Important Events in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Did you have the opportunity to leaf through it and to read it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, can you look through it now and read it, please. We are going to give you a little bit of time.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have looked at it briefly. The situation more or less was the way it is stated there, but I cannot confirm the specific events because at the time I was not familiar with the contents, and I did not have that in my unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. But are you able to confirm the actual events? For example, the attack on the JNA column in Sarajevo where 150 or 160 members of the JNA were massacred, that event is referred to in the document, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember that document, and we were all informed about it. It was an incident which actually strained to the extreme the relations between Serbs and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. The document also refers to the attack on the military column in Tuzla, do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about that because Major Brajic, Veljko Brajic was an operative in that regiment when they were handing over their arms and withdrawing. The Muslims attacked unarmed JNA soldiers, I don't know exactly how many of those soldiers were killed. That column was massacred.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Colonel Basara, in this document attacks on the JNA are dealt with in chronological order in the period that the document covers, just as it says. Can you confirm that this document could be a document by one of the military services or the military security organs?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was probably drafted with the help of the military organs that had this information at their disposal, that covered the entire territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I think that the witness sufficiently identified the origin and the source of the document for me to be able to ask that it be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, this is source for the goose, I am afraid. Yesterday when the colonel was asked to look at the document, the Sanski Most "Informator," my friend objected on the basis that he couldn't say it was accurate. All that he can say is that he heard about two of the events. That's all. Doesn't know who prepared the document, has never seen the document before. And so I am afraid at this stage, I don't think that there's sufficient foundation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: That is my instinctive view, but could I hear you further on Ms. Korner's objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may ...

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may help, can we just put it into evidence. Can we mark it for identification until we call military experts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You anticipate the decision of the Chamber. Yes, that is what we will do.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is now Exhibit 1D19, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Colonel Basara, it can be seen from this document that members of the JNA were continually attacked by weapons in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the period covered by the document; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who attacked members of the Yugoslav People's Army in Sarajevo, Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Sarajevo and Tuzla, they were attacked by Muslim forces that were armed and ready at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel Basara, what was the name of those paramilitary formations, do you have information about that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the information. All I know is the name Green Berets.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you know about the existence and organising of the patriotic league as armed formation of the party of democratic action?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did hear of it, but I didn't have any more specific information to be able to explain better to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, an intervention in the transcript. Page 10, line 18. It should have said Green Berets. The full name. I hope that has been corrected, and then we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Colonel, did you know that as early as 1991 in Western Herzegovina, the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosnia was formed?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did have information that it was formed in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that the Croatian democratic union was formed in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: But were you aware that there were some paramilitary formations of the Croatian HDZ party was formed?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Basara, would you agree with my conclusion that the Yugoslav People's Army was the target of attacks by those forces that were in favour of the break-up of the former Yugoslavia of separatism and fueled by the nationalist aspirations of some sections of the population?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Basara, now I'd like to come back to the part of the territory that you are more familiar with. Once on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina you received the assignment to take control of the area of Sanski Most; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do you know that that area was referred to as the Republic of Serbian Krajina, and that it was soon afterwards cut off from the rest of Republika Srpska in a part called the corridor?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I don't know if you know exactly for how long this lasted, until the middle of the summer, mid-July?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't be precise, but something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: During that time was there a threat of humanitarian catastrophe in Serbian Krajina? Was there a threat of a cut-off of electricity, supplies of food, medicines, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were attempts to stop the supplies and cut off power, but they never completely succeeded.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: There was wide media coverage of that case with 16 babies in the Banja Luka hospital who died only because the necessary oxygen could not be supplied, those were premature babies in neonatal units.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know about it at the time, but I found out later.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: But you know it happened during that break, the cut-off?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, people talked. I mean, there was a lot of talk about it among the Serbs, so I did find out.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Basara, military action followed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Would you be good enough to tell us where we are going with this?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You will find out, Your Honours, from my next question. The break-out through that corridor followed and a part of Colonel Basara's units participated. I want to ask him about that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Colonel Basara, you said yesterday, and I also found it in the interviews you gave, that one unit from your brigade took part in cutting that corridor?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one battalion participated under the command of Veljko Brajic, my Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You also said, and would you please confirm now, that when this battalion went to that part of the battle-field, it was placed under the command of the officer commanding that operation, and you no longer had command over him, or that unit; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Who was in command of this operation of cutting the corridor?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you precisely, but General Lisica and General Talic were most often mentioned in the reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So if your battalion entered a part of the area of responsibility under the command of General Lisica, you will agree with me that under the principle of resubordination, General Lisica would be in command of your unit?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do you know that General Lisica, for the requirements of that operation, mobilised also part of the Territorial Defence and the civilian police and placed them under his command?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the specifics of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: But do you know that this procedure is called resubordination?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I ask the legal officer to place the following document before the witness, 1D00-4042. May we see Article 104. We see only the cover page for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Colonel Basara, can you read this Article 104 now?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Is that the situation we are discussing now?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the situation, but the state of war had not been declared so this is not complete. But roughly that's what was envisaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Colonel Basara, in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the state of immediate threat of war had been declared on both parts of the territory, that controlled by the Muslims and Croats and that under the control of Serbs, and there was general across-the-board mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So it was not peacetime, there were wide-ranging military operations under way and one of them was the one we are discussing.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, since this is a regulation that we have referred to before, and we are going to refer to with other witnesses, in order to avoid discussing it separately with each witness, maybe we could tender it now, that's the law on national defence, and this particular witness is qualified to speak of this law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic and Ms. Korner, I may be wrong, but I seem to recollect that the parties had come to an agreement about a whole range of applicable laws from that period; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Almost. We were actually going to have a discussion this week about some of them, we had simply queried the relevance. But for the majority, as I say, provided they are relevant, we don't object. And I agree with Mr. Cvijetic on this, this is clearly a relevant document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So I wonder if it would be possible to admit in one batch simply all the law, so that we don't have to discuss admissibility of a law each and every time any of the parties bring up a law in front of the witness so that we simply can say that all the laws that are not in dispute between the parties are admissible or were taken --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, certainly I think we are all agreed on that. We were going to try to get together tomorrow, but if we are having the 65 ter meeting -- well, we could still probably do to afterwards, to try and sort this out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I agree with Ms. Korner, there's only one step we have to make to that end, and I think we should make it. Can I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Colonel Basara, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Will you please read Article 104 from the beginning. It says "in war" --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In war, in time of an immediate threat of war and in other emergencies" --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: That's enough. You admit that the immediate threat of war had been declared?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Then Article 104 applies, it's written in the law; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Colonel Basara, on the list of Prosecution exhibits, there's one which is an order which we have not had the opportunity to show you before.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll see with the Trial Chamber if it can be admitted, but I won't insist. It's from the 65 ter list 614, please. I'm not sure if we have the right document. Maybe if I give the ERN number, it will be easier to find. Sorry, 65 ter 1682.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's tab 7 in the Colonel's bundle from us.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Colonel, did you find it over there under tab 7? That's an order by Colonel Anicic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it's Colonel Anicic. We can see that at the beginning of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Okay. So you can see it. Look at the next page, 2. Paragraph 4. Para 4 on that page mentions the area of Sanski Most and your assignments.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where it says "I decided"?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: No, the following paragraph where it says, "engage the main forces," et cetera. It's the second paragraph of item 4. It says there that you have the right to resubordinate to the command of your brigade units of Territorial Defence as well.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's written there, and I was able to do that if I saw fit.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: That's precisely what we are discussing. If you resubordinate certain units as General Lisica did -- as Colonel Lisica did at the time, who has command over the units?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one who has units resubordinated to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: According to the principle of singleness of commands, that would be exclusively the military commander?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: My next set of questions relates to the responsibility --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Your Honour. May I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's already an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, did I understand you well, you didn't ask the witness whether he did resubordinate or not any police units to his unit? You asked him theoretically if he did so, but you didn't ask him whether he in practice did resubordinate, am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness replied that he had done that in keeping with this order, and that he had resubordinated to his command units of Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I did not say that because you didn't ask me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: But did you say you had done it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I said that is what is done when necessary if I see fit.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You mean you were able to do that if necessary?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was able, but in that case I hadn't done it because Colonel Anicic was not authorised to issue any orders to my brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe we have now clarified the situation to reply to the Judge's question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: But for the rest you stand by your answer?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that in principle that it was so. If there was a need on the ground, that's how it would be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Colonel Basara, if you had estimated that you needed certain units, both from the police and the Territorial Defence, you could have resubordinated them to yourself?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in agreement with the leadership of the municipality and the chief of MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In such a situation, who would be in command of the units? You just said that in a previous reply.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If some operations are underway, the one who has larger forces, stronger forces, would take over command.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Colonel Basara, the law explicitly says that the military command has overall command, and that all these units are resubordinated to military command.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because they are considered to be organised. They have an organised system of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And that fits with the system of singleness of command, you've just confirmed that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, I apologise for being confused a bit, but just in pursuit of the question put by Judge Delvoie, now we have established that the witness in his function as commander of the corps, he could have resubordinated local police units and units from the TO under his own command for the purpose of a particular combat operation. That, I think, is established, and this is perfectly within the law. The question was, did he ever in fact resubordinate police units and units from the TO under his command for any such purposes, and if so, in which cases?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think Colonel Basara heard your question. Maybe he could answer directly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While I was in command in Sanski Most, I never resubordinated units of the civilian police or the Territorial Defence under military command because there was no state of war, and I saw no need.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I managed to get the municipal leadership to accept them when I needed them into the complement of my brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: But you were able to do so under the law on immediate threat of war.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are right, but I never did it in practice because it wasn't necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You've answered the Judge's question. Colonel Basara, in the area of responsibility of your unit, your unit and resubordinated units alike, whenever a crime happened or a war crime perhaps, the perpetrator following this logic would be prosecuted by the military Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since no state of war had been declared, you cannot look at it that way because the main jurisdiction over the territory remained with the municipal leadership of Sanski Most because they had all the bodies in place. They ruled on that territory. We, the army, supplemented that work and secured territory --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: There is one extra microphone on, and we can't hear the witness that well anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Colonel Basara, in the area under the control of your unit, the military Prosecution authorities would have jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That depends on who perpetrated the crime since no state of war had been declared. If the perpetrator was a military person, a member of the brigade, then the military police would be in charge. If a civilian person committed the crime, then the SUP of Sanski Most would be in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about persons who have been mobilised who would qualify as military persons, military organs would have jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, members of the brigade, military authorities would have jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You keep repeating that the state of war had not been declared, but in your statement yesterday, on page 18 of your testimony yesterday, you said, I don't have full control on the territory since no state of war had been declared, apart from the part of the territory where my unit is deployed, there I have complete control did you state that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I knew full well that in the area of deployment of my units, I have control, but there is no definition of my area of responsibility. My superior did not define it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: To earlier questions why you filed no criminal complaints and why did you -- did not have such cases prosecuted, you answered that you did not have a technical service to assist you. However, that does not change jurisdiction. Military authorities exist, there is a military judge, there is a military prosecutor's office, all that exists in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, all these things existed, but you said yourself yesterday that these people were reserve forces, not professionals. They had just been mobilised. They were not qualified and trained to investigate. We made steps whenever we could, but there was so much to do that we did not have time for these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Still, did you have occasion to file a criminal complaint to the competent court regarding a crime committed on your territory?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, criminal complaints were filed. My chief of security and the police would file such criminal complaints, but I have no knowledge of it, and I cannot give you any names or cite any cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, I'll give you an example.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please show the witness one Defence exhibit, 2D07-0033.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Colonel Basara, do you see this criminal complaint?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not yet. We haven't found it yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You see on the screen the name of the person against whom this criminal complaint is filed. Can you read it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that it comes from the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think there's a problem. Neither -- I don't -- maybe the colonel or us have this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Colonel, please look at ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, sorry, it was a document -- Can you turn off your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 2D07-0033.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, it's in our -- it's actually in our binder. The colonel has that behind divider 22 in the bundle that he got from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, correct. We have found the document in the binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Colonel, have you found the document in the binder provided to you by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we have found it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Can you please turn to page 2 and look at the description of the events and what happened.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's clear, I'm familiar with that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Can you please turn to page 3. Who signed the criminal report?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: To whom did you send it to?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the Banja Luka military prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So there was a possibility of initiating proceedings before the relevant judicial bodies, and you used that opportunity; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we used the opportunity wherever we were able to establish the perpetrators. But when we could not establish who the perpetrators were, we were not able to submit criminal charges against unidentified perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, there is a procedure when you can submit criminal charges against unidentified perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is page 3 with Colonel Basara's signature. And then on page 2, if I'm not mistaken, there is the description of the event. Can we please look at page 2 on the e-court. Yes, here it is, but we don't see it in English so that His Honour can see it, so we also need to look at the previous page in the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: What I specifically wanted to know is what person it is this Prosecution is against. Is it the military? Is it a civilian?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Colonel, since you submitted the criminal report and you say that you recall this incident, can you please reply to the Judge's question?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a member of the 6th Krajina Brigade, and that is why the criminal report was submitted against him. Had he not been a member of the military, the charges would have been submitted to the Sanski Most MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Colonel Basara, if you don't know who the perpetrator of a crime is, then a criminal report would be submitted against unidentified perpetrators until the perpetrators were found, were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that at the time and that is why we did not submit criminal reports of that type.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: But this was your duty under the law; am I right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: To report about it and see if that can help to discover who the perpetrators were. However, that did not yield any results.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the regulations of the Federal Secretariat for National Defence about the application of the provisions of international law of war in the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, yes. And I think that I did adhere to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yes, but those provisions state that you would be responsible if you fail to submit a criminal report?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't specifically study those regulations. I didn't have time to really consider them in much detail. The command duties were very complex. I was the brigade commander for a period of time myself, so I didn't have an opportunity to do things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The gist of my question is that the fact that you were unable to do that at that particular time does not change your duties. At the time you were obliged to report to the prosecutor and initiate an investigation, and in this particular case this is what you did.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where there was a possibility that my unit or my men were involved, this is something that I did, but in circumstances where this was not possible, we did not do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right, Colonel Basara, at least we clarified what you were supposed to do. My next question refers to the events outside of the area of responsibility, for example, a member of the armed forces who was engaged and active in combat outside of the combat area in town, for example, perpetrates a crime or breaks the law, who is authorised to prosecute them?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the person who was in command of those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you that. I'm not asking you who their commander was. I'm saying whose duty was it to prosecute such persons? I'm thinking of organs in this case.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the question is not clear to me. Somebody commits some criminal act or crime somewhere, so I really am not able to tell you who would be authorised to prosecute them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, here, I'm going to try to help you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, again I apologise for interrupting you, but again I am not sure I understand the relevance of this evidence to the charges raised against your client. If I understand this correctly, Colonel Basara has confirmed that he had the authority to raise criminal charges against anyone under his command who had committed a serious crime, and we have seen that at least in one instance he actually did so. But how does this relate to the charges raised against Mr. Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Zupljanin are being charged with all the incidents and crimes that took place in the territories encompassed in the indictment, among other things pursuant to joint criminal enterprise, so we need to deal with the separation of authorities and duties between the civilian police and the army. So the gist of my questions is to see who is responsible for what, and I have specific documents in that sense about the division of jurisdiction between the police or the civilian organs, and the military organs. So I hope that you will permit me to deal with those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel Basara, before I put the question to you, I would like to ask that 65 ter list Exhibit number -- we are still looking at the previous document. 65 ter number 169, please. Can we see that on the screens. Can we just look at the English version as well, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Colonel Basara, are you able to see this document on the screen now?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It has to be in the binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Did you receive the document last night for your perusal?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. If not, then I'm just going to have to deal with interpretation of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry, are we on the right document? Because this is a document to do with Bijeljina, nothing whatsoever to do with this -- we are on the right document, are we? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Basara, can you please confirm that you have the document in front of you now?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document is in front of me now, but it's not quite clear to me what you are supposed to ask me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, I haven't managed to do that before I can make sure that you see the document. So in the area of Bijeljina, military personnel outside of the combat area, and you know that Bijeljina was never part of the combat zone, so if those persons commit some sort of a violation, a crime, were arrested and detained by the special unit of the civilian police. However, on the basis of this document we can see that the chief of intelligence, Colonel Zdravko Tolimir is sending a dispatch asking that the persons in question be handed over to the authorised military organs, and he even refers to provisions of the Law on the Army which state that the powers of the civilian and military organs are clearly delineated, and so on and so forth. Do you see that in his dispatch?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I suggest before I show the next document that is connected to this one, I would like to ask that this document be tendered as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I was waiting for what the question was going to be. Do you see it? Yes, I do. He doesn't know anything about this document. The contents are completely unknown to him. All he can say is, I've read it. And that's it. I'm sorry. In any event, I'm sure Mr. Cvijetic's document is going to come in as part of the Prosecution case, but this witness simply cannot say anything about this document. And, indeed, if any further documents are going to be shown to him about which he knows nothing on an area which isn't an area he covered, all he can be asked to do is read it or comment, then I suggest that Mr. Cvijetic leaves it and moves on to something the witness actually can deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'm going to continue along that line, and then we will see whether we will stay with the option of tendering them or marking them for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Colonel Basara, as we can see, Zdravko Tolimir is protesting the arrest of the military persons and is seeking that they be handed over to military authorities. Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says there. That is his understanding of matters, and he decided to act in that particular way.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at the next document to see how the minister of the interior acted in terms -- or in relation to that dispatch.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, but this is just not the witness for these documents to be brought in. He has not seen them. He doesn't know anything about it. It is not within his sphere of competence at all. I'm quite happy to let documents go in normally, provided the witness can say something. But, really, this witness cannot comment on any of these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, and this applies to Colonel Basara as well, this is a matter of the application of regulations, not about the conduct of any particular senior officer. It deals with the delineation of authorities between the civilian and the military organs, and that's what it says. So it cannot be left up to the discretion of Colonel Zdravko Tolimir or to the minister of internal affairs to apply regulations as they see fit. Regulations require that they be applied in the way stated in the correspondence between the two parties. So if the military personnel -- I'm asking the witness about the circumstances about the delineation of powers and did that apply in the way described in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Colonel Basara, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Did you hear this explanation that I provided? In this specific case we are talking about the application of the law --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you something about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The witness said -- he answered. He explained how he applied whatever rule you are putting to him. He said, I exert my authority on military and not on all of personnel, on all of persons. So what is the use -- what is the use of your line of questions? Sorry, but I can't see it. If he was wrong, okay, then he was wrong, in your view. But that's the way how he did it. That's his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I agree with you. The witness is mistaken, but I'm trying to prove to him that he is wrong. And how am I to prove that if --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic can prove this through other witnesses who are coming as part of the Prosecution case or when it comes to his own case. He cannot go behind the witness's answers by showing the witness documents that the witness knows nothing about. That's the objection, and I suggest that Mr. Cvijetic moves on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, the -- you've asked the witness questions, he has answered to the best -- you may or may not accept the answers. To the extent that it is a part of your case that you are challenging him on this, you may be able to do it at some stage but not by putting in this document at this stage because the witness says he knows nothing about it. He has never seen it before. And I think that's as far as you can go with this document. You've asked the witness a question, and he has answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Your Honours. I'm being told that it's time for a break, and if you agree, I would like to perhaps stop here and then we can continue after the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, can I just ask, it's a question of the witness who is still waiting for -- to be cross-examined. Is he likely to be required today? Because he is going to be brought over around 12.00, but at the rate we are going ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Depends on Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Mr. Cvijetic, actually, I don't know how much longer he has got.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, how long time do you think you need to complete your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not more than half an hour, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, counsel. And Mr. Pantelic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would estimate that -- well depending of the transmission problems and the dynamic how it works, my colleague Cvijetic covered a significant part of the issues, but I would say maybe one hour and a half. I will do my best maybe to shorten the time, but that should be roughly hour and a half for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, counsel. This seems to indicate that there will be about half an hour in the end in which we could actually continue the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We'll have him brought over for 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Colonel, are you ready to continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am. I thought you were asking the colonel if he is still on line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I was, I didn't hear a response. I don't know if there is a problem. Colonel, can you hear us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't have to admit this document, we agreed amongst ourselves, we won't insist.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I would just like to ask the colonel on this document, who is Colonel Zdravko Tolimir, the signatory?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know Colonel Tolimir, and I did not collaborate with him. However, I would like to explain something about competencies and jurisdictions here.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Will you just answer my question. Who is Colonel Zdravko Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You don't know that he was member of the staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, chief of the security section?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And you don't know that in the hierarchy of the VRS, he was your superior, just as the entire staff was your superior?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know him, and I can't tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: How do you know, then, who the supreme commander of the VRS was, if you know?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's a ridiculous question. Of course I know, and I know whose orders I was carrying out, and that was enough for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You won't tell me that instructions and orders by Colonel Tolimir did not reach your unit.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They probably went to the corps, but down at the level of my unit, I didn't see any of those orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: What does it mean to you if I say that Colonel Zdravko Tolimir could have been the chief of security for the entire VRS?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll take your word for it, but at the time I did not know that he was the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: On the same document, my last question, I owe an answer to the Chamber why the document is relevant; namely, Colonel Zdravko Tolimir was chief of security in the Main Staff of the VRS, and his instructions on the application of regulations and the division of competencies in jurisdiction applied throughout the Republika Srpska. But I won't insist if the witness does not wish to comment any further, and I agree to have the document admitted through another witness. May I continue, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Colonel, another question remains that I would like to deal with. If I'm not mistaken, the Army of Republika Srpska was established on 19 May?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall the exact date because I was engaged full time, and we had no particular communications about that, so I can't tell you the dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You say there was no notification. Was that in the period when communications were severed, when power was cut off?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the time. I can't answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: But did you become a commanding officer in the VRS?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must have been since I had command of a brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Can we at least agree about the month, that it was May?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can agree if you have documents confirming the date when the main leadership of Republika Srpska made the decision. Of course I can accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. I have a few questions about the origin of the VRS. The Yugoslav People's Army was ordered to leave the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina at one point; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And it was mainly JNA officers who were natives of Bosnia and Herzegovina who remained after JNA withdrawal.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Conscripts who responded to the call-up joined their own armies in the war.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And the Muslims who were in the JNA previously joined their own people which formed its own army.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, most of them. There were some who remained in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Sefer Halilovic, whose rank I don't know, was Chief of Staff of the BH Army, he was a former JNA officer; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know the man, so I can't tell you with any certainty, but I heard that he was a former JNA officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. Have you heard of the commander of the 5th Corps, Atif Dudakovic, that he, too, was a former JNA officer before joining the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well then you will agree with my conclusion that the Yugoslav People's Army ripped at the ethnic seams on which it had been established, and both officers and troops joined their own peoples and their armies.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: But by it's own concept the VRS had in its ranks both Croats and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning, yes, but they left later.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you said that they left because they accepted an invitation from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not mean that it was an invitation. Directives came from Sarajevo that Muslim troops and officers should leave the JNA so that the JNA remain a mono-ethnic force, purely Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I have documents that these appeals were made by political parties, the HDZ on the Croatian side, and SDA on the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in the eastern Bosnian corps, there was one whole unit, a brigade consisting of Muslims and Croats, some of them were officers and some of them received decorations for their achievements in war?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Colonel Basara. My name is Igor Pantelic. I'm waving here. Can you see me?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We met last Sunday on the premises of the field -- of the office of The Hague Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: On that occasion we spoke in the presence of a representative of the OTP and an interpreter; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You spoke of yourself as a tolerant man, and that's the impression I had too.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I reckon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You were one of the founders of the movement called the National Front for Yugoslavia which rallied humanists.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You were a co-founder with some of your friends and colleagues of Muslim ethnicity; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: How would you prefer to be addressed because there is a military etiquette, Colonel sir, or Comrade Colonel?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Comrade Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I accept that. Comrade Colonel, would you tell me if you had any knowledge of the grouping of Muslim forces in the area of Sanski Most in a place called "Suma" Golaja, woods Golaja?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had information they had a training centre there, with around 400 Green Berets.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When did you get that information, approximately? In which month of 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you exactly, but it would have been May.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When we spoke in Belgrade on Sunday, you mentioned you had information that there had been frequent helicopter flights in the area of that forest, Golaja, around that training centre, and that there were indicia that reinforcements -- that is, personnel and goods were air-lifted there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: According to your information, the commander of that unit was a certain Captain Avdic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you know his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In the course of 1992, did you have occasion to meet him?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met him on my command post when he came together with his Chief of Staff. And he even spent the night at my command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What were the circumstances in which a commander of the enemy force would visit your command post and even spend the night there? How did it come about?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time we had organised a search operation of that forest because we had information there was a training centre. Our units carried out a circular movement towards the centre of the forest. However, two soldiers were inebriated, they burst in front of a firing squad before the Muslims, and they were captured. And then the battalion commander went to negotiate with the opposite side. He had with him a signalsman and means of communication. He, too, was captured together with the signalsman. And then they interfered with the command system. My Chief of Staff, Major Brajic, first managed to set up contact with Captain Avdic. They discussed the matter, and Avdic said he would release our men on the condition that we transport them to Bihac. I told him to come to my command post to talk to me, so he did. And we came to an agreement, and since it was already late, he spent the night and left the next day. The next day we acted upon our agreement and 160 troops who had not dispersed from that forest who were still there were also shipped to Bihac. We informed the UNPROFOR, and no one came to any harm.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So to summarise, you had an understanding with the Green Berets that once your negotiations were over you would transport them to their own territory in Bihac, and that agreement was implemented; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let us go back to the general context in Sanski Most. You mentioned that it was your general impression that certain anxiety prevailed among the Serb population, anxiety and fear that they could meet the same fate as their ancestors in the Second World War, and the fate of their ancestors were tragic because Serbs suffered a lot under both Croat, Muslim, and Ustasha units, and many were killed?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When you came to Sanski Most, I suppose you tried to gather as much information as you could about the situation on the ground. What kind of knowledge did you gain about inter-ethnic relations in that area? Briefly.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information I received was often frightening. There were indicia that units were being formed everywhere. There was information that Muslim forces were present in Mahala, which means in Sanski Most. Then there were those units and training centres in Golaja and also units in Hrustovo. Hrustovo is closely linked with this Golaja location, and the units in Hrustovo probably got their supplies from the training centre in Golaja.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I understand that, but did you have information about the mutual links and coordination between these three groupings of Muslim forces, Mahala, Golaja, and Hrustovo?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we had information that they were interlinked, Golaja and Hrustovo, Hrustovo and Mahala. They were also linked by other areas, but some of them were cut-off from each other by my units, which prevented closer linkage.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That's clear now. Tell me, your command post was practically in Glusci village, Palanka; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I'm waiting for the transcript to catch up.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [In English] I will spell the name of village where the commanding post was. It's G-l-u-s-c-i, and then second name is P-a-l-a-n-k-a. For the precision in transcript, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tell me, Colonel, you were born in village Glusci Palanka?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually in the village of Otis near Glusci Palanka.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When you returned to your native area in 1992, you must have had personal contact with friends, relatives. You had a network of friends, I suppose, and you socialised with them?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: How did your friends and family explain to you the situation on the ground in mixed population localities where there were both Muslims and Serbs living in the same area?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was anxiety and concern, but for the most part they said they had no problem with immediate neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And now about the 6th Brigade. You said that its numbers were 3 and a half thousand to 4.000 in July/August; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And you, as brigade commander, had assistance -- let's take them one by one. First of all, you had the Chief of Staff whom you mentioned today, Major Veljko Brajic; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he arrived in early May after the attack on the army column in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Then you had an assistant commander for morale, and religious affairs, Brane Davidovic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was a reserve officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What was his rank?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Captain first class.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And your assistant commander for security was Pero Malinovic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Malicevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Pero Malicevic, is it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: His rank?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Captain 1st class reserve.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And his assistant was Branko Vukmir?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What was his rank?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Also captain 1st class, reserve officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your assistant commander for logistics was Colonel Kuljaca; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was Lieutenant-Colonel Kuljaca, retired JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And the chief of engineering, you can't recall his name?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I had three of them at various times. I can't recall their name.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: While you were stationed in Croatia, in Jasenovac, your assistant for security was Mirko Vrucinic, captain; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, my chief for intelligence was Mirko Vrucinic, not for security, but for intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And what was his rank there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Captain 1st class. A reserve officer, non-commissioned officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I assume that you had professional cooperation and relations with this person?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When your brigade was transferred to the Sanski Most region, Mirko Vrucinic continued to be your assistant for intelligence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for awhile that was so, but I don't remember at which point they asked me to release him so that he could be the chief of the MUP, and I approved that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Who specifically asked that he be the MUP chief candidate in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a request by the president of the municipality, Rasula.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And you agreed because in your view he was a good professional, and you believed that that would be a good cadre solution?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I considered him to be a good man, somebody who was not a nationalist, and I felt that he would be carrying out those duties well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Specifically because he came from your unit, and because you were -- you held him in high esteem, you had a good opinion of him. During your stay in Sanski Most, you had good professional cooperation with him; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, our cooperation was excellent because whenever we could, we cooperated and helped each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I will have to make a pause, it's not that I don't know what I'm going to ask you next; I'm just considering the pace and paying attention to the transcript, so I'm grateful for your patience. And you exchanged operative data with Mirko Vrucinic about enemy actions, the situation in the field; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Of course you as a conscientious commander of a unit reported to Vrucinic certain negative things in your brigade?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever we met, we discussed all the problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Including some negative occurrences, violations, criminal acts, some abuses, did you discuss all of these matters with him?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I discussed with him all matters that I considered that he should be informed about.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. Along the security line, your assistant, Pero Malicevic was directly reporting to Colonel Bogovic in the 1st Krajina Corps in Banja Luka; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And one of his duties was that he should report to his superior officer along that line on matters that had to do with his tasks?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And this implied reporting to superior military organs, some omissions or some abuses of authority or desertion or violations of military discipline or criminal acts or killings; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were two lines of reporting, the line of operative duty where there was an officer on duty each day who compiled all that information and sent it to the operation duty officer in the corps. Along -- the intelligence officer would send all of the information compiled to the security chief in the corps if he felt that he should have such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So your assistant informed his superior about the events in Mahala.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably the reports did go out. I can't say what was exactly in them and when they were sent, but they were definitely sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. Let me be specific for the transcript; it wasn't entered correctly. I asked you if your security assistant informed the killings in Mahala -- of the killing of the Muslim population, and he sent that information to his superior; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In the beginning in your brigade you had a platoon of the military police which was later a company of the military police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: How many men were in this military police company?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 90, but this was subject to change.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The commander of that company was a lieutenant from Prijedor; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Lieutenant Madzar. And then later someone else came. I can't remember that person's last name. He came there and then took over as the company commander when I left the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So we are talking about 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, in view of your humanism and a proper approach to matters, could you please tell the Trial Chamber how you managed to take a son of a Muslim friend of yours who was wearing military policemen's uniform, you practically managed to save this man when his father asked you to do that. How did you manage to get him across to Serbia? How did that happen?
