What were your motives to dress this young man into a military policeman's uniform, transfer him to Serbia, from where he later went to Europe. Can you please tell us about that.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is not just any Muslim, the son of a Muslim. It's actually captain Nijaz Halilovic who was commander of the TO staff in Sanski Most. When I came to the Sanski Most area, he toured all of the Muslim villages with me and we talked with all the Muslims in all the Muslim villages in that area, and we asked them to refrain from any activities involving weapons in that area and that the two of us would do our best to secure peace and things as they had been up until then. However, later when there was an escalation and there was the division of the MUP and also the division of power took place, and also when this commander was replaced, this commander of the TO staff was replaced by Colonel Anicic. I went to visit my family in Belgrade, and he had been arrested and sent to Manjaca. When I returned I met his father and he said, What will happen to Nijaz? I said that it was my duty to transfer Nijaz to him in Austria where he had a permanent labour permit, that I would get him out of Manjaca and send him to his father. And this is what I did. In order to be able to do that, I had to find a way because they didn't allow able-bodied Muslim men to cross the border into Serbia. I dressed him in the uniform of a policeman, and he was my escort. And then when he crossed over into Serbia, he put on civilian clothing, and then he left for Austria.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And where was Captain Nijaz Halilovic when you did this? Was he in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he wasn't in Sanski Most. He was in the Manjaca camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I think that you mentioned, or perhaps this was in the interview with the Prosecution. You practically came to Manjaca accompanied by a military judge, and that's how you did it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was accompanied by Judge Mirko Adamovic when I went to Manjaca, and I had a decision to release this person, after which I took over custody.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And this does not seem to be the only example of you intervening in this humanitarian way. I think that I read somewhere that you personally, or not you personally, but you had sent some soldiers of yours to release some Muslims pursuant to a request by their parents; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were four Muslims from Krupa who were detained after the actions in Krupa. They were detained in the school. I was asked by this man called Fajdo Kurbegovic with whom I had dealt with before from Kamengrad. He said that there was the mother and two sons in there, that they were of a Yugoslav orientation, they were not extremists, so I was asked if I could make sure that those people went and -- to stay with their mother. So I took the two of them and two others who had guaranteed that they were of the Yugoslav orientation. I took all of them to Kamengrad, and I handed them over to Fajdo Kurbegovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: This is all very interesting and noble of the witness having saved lives of Muslims during the conflict, but I want to be sure that we spend the time in addressing issues that are directly relevant to your client's case, so please help me out in explaining to me the relevance of these incidents, as much as I find them interesting and, as I said, very noble of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I absolutely agree with you, and I'm sharing your opinion that these are very noble examples and actions of Comrade Colonel. And I'm now leaving this topic. It will be just a part of an overall line of my cross-examination, and I will be more than happy to give you a more precise answer after the cross-examination or about the end of cross-examination, and I'm very mindful of the directives. Thank you so much. Just --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If it helps, I think it's extremely relevant, not perhaps for the reasons that Mr. Pantelic is putting forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I don't want to say why is now, because you can understand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, sir, I'm going to put a couple of questions to you now about the commander of the paramilitary formation with the name SOS about a certain Njunja. Yesterday while providing answers to questions by the Prosecutor, you mentioned this Njunja; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When we spoke in Belgrade, you and I, in the presence of OTP representatives, you said that this Njunja was someone who was both feared by the police and the military as well as the civilians in Sanski Most, Njunja and his men; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: He had a, let's say, sizeable group of seasoned fighters under his command from various fronts; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: He also had serious weaponry, including three-barrelled guns; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: This was a three-barrelled anti-aircraft gun that he had seized or acquired in some other way from the military depot in Bihac; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At Grabez.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. Grabez is close to Bihac; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, near Bihac and probably this is where he obtained it from.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You as the commander of the brigade in the area of responsibility of your brigade wanted to introduce or impose a certain degree of discipline, so for those purposes, you placed him under the command of your brigade and you managed to control him, like you told me in Belgrade, to an extent of 50 per cent. You managed to impose 50 per cent of control over him and his men.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I kind of calmed down the activities of that unit to a degree of 50 per cent, making them respect the system of command and discipline and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When you said you managed to calm down their activities, this referred to stopping their behaving inappropriately, their abuses in committing violations?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were the cause of fear among the population. They boasted that they were some sort of powerful group, and then to a certain degree, I managed to reduce this activity of theirs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But there is that remaining 50 per cent. You said that you had brought them under control to an extent of 50 per cent. What about the other 50 per cent? Can you tell the Trial Chamber about that.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was difficult. I was not able to control them completely because they always evaded control.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did they want to leave the unit, just like the most of us did when we were in the army, we wanted to go off and have a beer or two or have fun with girls and things like that? Or did they commit more serious thing, did they commit robberies, rapes, any other kinds of crimes? What specifically did you mean?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any specific information about the crimes they committed. I don't have that information at my disposal. If they did commit something somewhere, they did it so skillfully that it was not possible to blame them for it. For example, when they went to the front within a battalion, two or three days later they would come back, then they would go again when they felt like it, and that's how they behaved.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Trial Chamber where was that unit that was under some type of your control? Where did they go to the front? To which sectors of the front?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They went in the action when they were breaking through to the corridor. Then they went to Gradacac, Bosanski Brod. More or less it was those sectors of the front that they went to.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And members of SOS, did they take part in actions in Mahala?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't engage them there because at that time they were not subordinated to me, so I don't really have information about that. But most probably they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did they take part in the operations in Hrustovo?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did they take part in the actions in Golaja against the Green Berets?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, now we are going to move to another topic, and this is this relationship with the police where your colleague Vrucinic was the head. In Belgrade you confirmed to me that you never met or saw my client Mr. Stojan Zupljanin; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You also told me that in certain situations when needed for purposes of the service, that the military police from the 1st Krajina Corps and the security organs would come to Sanski Most to carry out certain investigations in cooperation with your security assistant; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the circumstances, when would they come, what was the subject of their investigation?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't really tell you specifically, but when the Serbs organised the attack on Sanski Most, they found themselves in the hotel in Sanski Most, a platoon of that military police from Banja Luka, and they helped us to pull out the MUP across the Sana without any losses.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I think that you spoke about issuing an order that some parts of your brigade go to some combat assignments in Kljuc; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Not combat assignments, but they should provide security and prevent conflicts during the take-over of power in Kljuc by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And on that occasion, I must say, when you were explaining that to me in Belgrade, it was my impression that this was -- that you as a brave and capable commander -- perhaps you can tell the Trial Chamber about that episode when the Serbian soldiers fired into the air in front of the building where you were sitting with Colonel Galic and other military officials at the time. How did you deal with the situation? How did you react?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I had been carrying out command duties all my life and had been in command of the army. I had -- or in command of soldiers, I had more experience than the people who were with me, and when I was attending this meeting, Colonel Galic, who was the commander of that division, was also there. One battalion was supposed to go to the front, they were in vehicles, and they were expected to leave shortly, but then mass firing broke out so that we were unable to go on with the meeting. The president of the municipality asked Colonel Galic, since he was the person that was most responsible to go outside and to stop this firing. He said that he wasn't crazy to go outside and get killed. Then he addressed the brigade commander, and he also said no one can stop these men. I went out and I toured the column of parked military vehicles. I introduced myself to them. And I calmly asked them not to fire and they stopped firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. I understood that. And then a part of your brigade which was then stationed in Kljuc, went back to Sanski Most together with you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, you didn't understand me. Not then because by that time -- actually, this was done before. My units were there earlier. Already by the time we had had that meeting, there was already the Serbian municipality of Kljuc established, and that is the meeting that I was attending. At that time my unit wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. I think you told this to the Prosecution in the interviews you had with them, in response to an investigator if you had been informing the Superior Command about certain orders that you had issued about the transfer of parts of units in that area, you said, No, there was no need for that. You made decisions about that as a professional soldier, about where you would transfer which part of your brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't report about that because there were no combat activities at the time. There were no losses. And I didn't have any need to do that because I didn't want to seem to be boasting with any kind of results or my achievements. And I mainly had the attitude that this was something normal, that was part of my duties, and it was not necessary to report on it particularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And did you transfer your brigade or parts of your brigade to specific parts of the front pursuant to some evaluations of yours without reporting to the Superior Command?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not bigger units, perhaps smaller units up to the strength of a platoon. I would send them to help others. That's what I did. As for a battalion that I had sent to the area between Bosanska Krupa and Bihac, it's a wood called Alibegovica Kosa where the Green Berets used to set up ambushes frequently there to fighters of the Petrovac Brigade, nobody dared enter those woods. So I asked the corps commander to allow me and a battalion of mine to go to that area so that we could secure that area between the Krupa and Petrovac Brigade. This was done at the time and stayed in force right until Oluja, that part of the forest.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We've talked before, and I've also studied it in your previous statements, you claim that your relationship with municipal authorities was not really a friendly one.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not friendly because they were trying to place me under their command. And there were many of their own units, some sort of municipal army, I was informed of that. And I did not accept even to be a member of their Crisis Staff as they had wanted me to. They wanted me to be a member of the Crisis Staff, and in that way get command over me and my brigade. But I did not accept that, and I did not accept any interference in my command by politicians.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So let us summarise. You say that you planned and carried out all your military operations and never allowed anyone to interfere in your professional job?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: On the territory of the Sanski Most municipality, there was a unit of Territorial Defence; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were two TO battalions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: How were these two battalions armed? What did they have?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The usual weaponry the Territorial Defence used to have, light weaponry. They had a limited number of 82 and 60 millimetre mortars and the light weapons, infantry weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I understood you as saying that, as required, you sometimes included these two Territorial Defence battalions in your combat operations?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not include them as required. At a later stage, I managed to agree with Rasula to have these two battalions join the 6th Brigade, and once they were part of the brigade, they took part in all our actions, just as all the rest of the troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Of course, under your command.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You said to me that losses, human losses in 1992 in your brigade were 12 soldiers, although I seem to have read somewhere that it was 15. But those total losses in 1992, let's agree, were between 11 and 15. We are not talking about the wounded now.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whoever wrote this was wrong. Only 11 of my men got killed in combat around Hrustovo and Golaja. And there were 123 dead in all at the time when I left the brigade, that's towards the end of 1992. And that included combat in other theatres of war where my battalions took part, so the total is 123.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you have any knowledge or information that during the attack on Mahala and segments of the Muslim populace were in contact with those Muslim units in Golaja just before the attack on Mahala?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: For awhile before this problem with Mahala occurred, there was sporadic fighting across the Sana river between Sanski Most and Golaja. And these skirmishes were mostly on the part of the SOS, those armed units in Mahala. I had information they were linked with Golaja via Hrustovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So we can agree that armed Muslim elements in Mahala in coordination with their own units in Golaja were, at that time, members of the enemy force; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: For the transcript, I'm asking you, they were members of the enemy army for all practical purposes; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm following the transcript again. These computers, you know. It's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now, the principal aim of the military operation in Mahala was to disarm citizens who illegally owned weapons?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: On that occasion following the principles instilled in you as a trained commander, you gave those Muslim armed citizens and others an ultimatum and a dead-line of three hours to surrender their weapons, failing which a military operation would ensue?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you got me wrong. I gave three hours to the populace that all those who don't want to fight surrender their weapons and leave across a plateau called Pijesci [phoen] where my forces would be stationed and would make sure that nobody comes to any harm. So I gave three hours to all those who don't want to resist our forces to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And as far as you remember, how many civilians left?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very large numbers. And when we realised there were many people in that area, we escorted them towards Dana [phoen] village and down further on towards Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And those who remained in Mahala were considered as members of the enemy army?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because they didn't want to pull out. And if combat operations followed, nobody can guarantee their safety any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Were there any civilian casualties on the Muslim side during that operation?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no figures about casualties because I was taken elsewhere by other duties. Whether any specific figures existed, I don't know. But the civilian protection people who conducted the sanitisation in that area of the terrain may have information.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: For the transcript, could you explain this term "sanitisation of the terrain"?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under JNA regulations there was a body called civilian protection in every municipality. There would be one unit of civilian protection in every municipality. If any combat operations occur, when they are finished, they combed the terrain. If they find any wounded in the battle-field, they transport them to the health centre, and they bury bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Of course after a military operation, the commander in charge is the one who issues the order for sanitisation.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in this case, the civilian protection was not under my command, so they must have gotten their orders from the municipal authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Another military operation you mentioned was in the village of Hrustovo, two of your soldiers were killed there.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Four were killed in Hrustovo. At the beginning when the unit approached the village of Hrustovo, two men were killed. Then the commander pulled the unit back and organised an attack on Hrustovo, but still, he gave them two hours. First of all, he found out that there were some people who were armed there and then he gave two hours to women, children, and the elderly, and those who don't want to fight to leave the village and go to Vrhpolje. And after those two hours, the attack began. And in the attack another two men were killed. So a total of four died at Hrustovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It seems around 30 civilians including small children and one infant were killed in a garage in Hrustovo. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That information never reached me, but if it had happened then at Hrustovo, the battalion commander certainly would have informed me if it had happened that day. Now, whether something like that happened later, after the unit withdrew, I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor also asked you for a comment on the forensic report that the victims of that incident were killed with automatic rifles?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My unit was not informed of that. My assistant commanders were not informed of that. I did not know about it so I cannot provide a comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now, after that -- after that operation when some inhabitants of that village, young women or girls seemed to have been transporting bodies to bury them, it seems they were targeted by mortar fire. Who fired from the mortars?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my units were not there, so my units could not have fired mortars on that area. Then I suppose, because I was not an eye-witness, I suppose that the Muslims in Golaja might have fired by mistake at people moving across that area because only they from Golaja had enough mortar range.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could I ask for the page number in the interview that you are putting to him? And is it the first or the second?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It's the second one. It's interview from March this year.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Page?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Page ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, it's time for the break so maybe you can look for the page number and then give it to us as soon as we resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: During the break -- can I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: During the break, I checked the statement which was gave by this witness, it's a page 45 of an interview of 31st of March this year. And OTP investigator, Mr. Grady put to the witness, this is the end of that page, put -- they are speaking about the events in Hrustovo, and then Mr. Grady said to Colonel Basara, I will quote: "No, no, mortars. So they couldn't bury the bodies in the Muslim fashion. Colonel, we've exhumed all the bodies. They were all shot to death by automatic rifles, and there is a witness to this crime" -- sorry, to "the crime." "And your forces -- your forces, the 6th Sana Brigade launched that attack on Hrustovo after two Serb soldiers were killed." And then Colonel Basara is explaining, you know, stuff. So this is the particular portion which I made reference. Thank you. In relation to the armaments, the use of particular type of gun. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Comrade Colonel, in Belgrade, you mentioned to me that in 1992, you had lots of suspicions about your Chief of Staff Brajic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When your memory was fresher, because now it's 17 years after the event and you gave your interview to the Prosecution in 2002, when talking about the situation around the mosque, you said the Chief of Staff ordered the destruction of the mosque to the chief of engineering, you said it was Brajic.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Then you intervened, you said it was not all right, and you said you used the ruse. How did you get that information? Very wisely, cunningly. You shook hands with him and said, Good job, well done. And he chuckled and he said, Ha, I didn't even need much explosive. Do you remember saying that to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you have indicia that Brajic was involved in other such operations? Because the use of explosives needs some training.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I had no indications of his involvement. But the way he acted in field operations, in taverns, in bars, I had an inkling who he is fraternising with, I knew he was slandering me as a commander, and I concluded that he -- his intention was to disqualify me as a commander so as to take over command himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Let's go back to this incident in Hrustovo when the Prosecutor, in fact the investigator, Mr. Grady, asked you in March this year whether the police was involved in the attack in Hrustovo, you said no.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Colonel, let's go briefly through a few documents. The first one I'd like you to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The first one was put recently in e-court the reference is 2D07-0045. And for the benefit of our colleagues in Belgrade ICTY office, this document is mentioned in our mail under the title "Additional Document for Use with Witness ST-203."

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe this will be shown to you now. The thing is that the command of the 1st Krajina Corps gave an order, document dated 23rd June 1992. Okay. Do you see this document, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I'd like to know about this part here. In the first paragraph item 1. It's an instruction saying that retaliatory action against the innocent and helpless Serbian population must be prevented. And further down it says that some cases had already happened and, therefore, measures of maximum efficiency must be taken to put an end to this and prevent further such happenings. Now, on the second page of this document -- do you have two pages?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can we have the other page of the same document, please. In e-court it's 01029826. The second page of this document. Madam Registrar, can we -- okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just say to whom this was sent. This is, by the way, a Prosecution document because we, in the Defence, have nothing. They have grabbed everything, and we can only use their documents. You see this is this 9th Partisan Division. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now, what I want to ask you is this: First, do you remember such instructions handed down from the Superior Command? I see that you carried it out in the field as a conscientious soldier. Do you have knowledge of this order?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, concerning this specific one, I can't say that I'm very familiar with it because it was a long time ago. But what is written in this order was frequently imparted to us at all meetings in the corps command. We were always told that we must take measures to this end to prevent torchings, violence, looting, and we did what we could, to the extent of our capacity.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we have exhibit number for this document, please. If there is no objections from Prosecution side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Has it been exhibited previously?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: That's fine, Mr. Pantelic. But I can't see it on the screen. Do you have a date and a providence?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's the first page, Your Honour. I would kindly ask Madam Registrar to show us the first page of this document, where it's 1st Krajina Corps command, 23rd of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will become Exhibit 2D15, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You have a binder there, Colonel, given to you by the Prosecution. Under tab 29 is your order of the 1st of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: This is ERN number 0069834 and 35. This is the order of Colonel Basara dated 1st of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, can I also remind you that I think you have about 20 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but, please, I kindly ask not to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. We can't hear Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I kindly ask for understanding if we have these technical problems, that it will not be count, please. Okay. Thank you so much. So now we have B/C/S version on the left side.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel Basara, do you have there in Belgrade this order you issued on the 1st of June? Do you have it in front of you? Is that all right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So you confirm then that in the top left corner, the date is 1st of June, 1992, the command of the 6th Partisan Brigade, Donji Tramosnja village, and the signature is yours. You confirm the authenticity of this document and your signature?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. The point of this document is what had been suggested by the Superior Command, and you now convey this to your units briefly, that it's necessary to arrest and remove all troops who do not comply with regulations. Second, that errors allowed previously in the treatment of prisoners must not be repeated. Three, that no crimes must be committed against women, children, and the elderly. Four, that a military court, a marshal court be created at the level of the brigade. And five, that paramilitaries and other irregulars be prevented from entering the area of the brigade because they -- their purpose is looting. Do you remember this order?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This order was written actually in order to be read out to the troops to warn them once again that some omissions that had been allowed before must not be repeated. All this was done, in fact, save for the fact that the corps command did not allow me to set up a marshal court because no state of war had been declared, but still the troops thought that it had, and this helped improve discipline in the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So from the 1st of June onwards, you managed to put this under control?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think there were any crimes on that territory after this date. Everything that happened happened before.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we have a number for this exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour if it helps, it's on our 65 ter list as well, although I didn't use it, but, I mean, you may as well -- you know, the Defence can use it as a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 2D16, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, excuse me for interrupting, but I thought you were saying that the previous document, the previous document was prior to this one, but this one is prior to the order of the high command.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, my explanation to witness actually was that knowing that he was acting in accordance with the principles of law, he, actually, before the particular order, which came from 1st Krajina Corps, he already on the field in his zone of responsibility acted fully in accordance -- in fact I would say that Colonel Basara was a kind of -- he was -- he predicted what will come because he is a professional, highly-educated officer, so, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yeah, you are welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, excuse me. I'd like to ask you about a few things. Would you agree with me that on the territory of Sanski Most municipality your brigade followed -- following orders from the Superior Command carried out actions of disarmament and seizure of illegally-owned weapons regardless of ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, regardless of ethnicity. Both Serbs who had weapons and illegal possessions and others were brought in and taken into custody and whenever we had information that there were illegally-owned weapons, we acted upon that information and such weapons were seized.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I studied a bit some of your communications and dispatches, and I talked to your colleagues from the area, and maybe you will confirm what I say now. In this period, we are talking about early June, the process of disarming people. Is it the case that in Lusci Palanka, Dana, the left bank, Dabar, Koprivna, and Ostra Luka in the territory of Sanski Most were all subject to this disarmament procedure?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This disarmament action was not conducted as a consistent operation, but whenever we had information that somebody had weapons in illegal possession, that person was brought into the brigade. Those weapons were either seized from the person or the person joined the brigade if they so wished.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just answer briefly yes or no. Did these activities take place in the region of Budimlic Japra, Lusci Palanka, Sanski Most, left bank, and Koprivna; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Budimlic, no; and in all the other places, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You are an educated officer, please tell me this, were any combat activities conducted using the main force along the axis of Skucani Vakuf, Kamengradska Dolina, Sanski Most, Vrhpolje? Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no combat there, no combat activities were carried out there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Were there any artillery preparations against Mahala carried out?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no artillery preparation was done. Only when it was discovered that there was mortar fire from the Mahala broader area, mortar fire was opened and support given to units that were moving towards the centre of Mahala.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So you agree that there was artillery fire on Mahala; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was. Once it was discovered that they also were firing from mortars because at the time one of my officers was wounded from a mortar shell that was fired precisely from that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And now can you tell me whether the units were deployed in Dabar, Lusci Palanka, Budimlic Japra, Koprivna, Ostra Luka, and Usorci? Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why you are including Budimlic Japra. We had nothing in Budimlic Japra.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And the rest?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The forces were deployed in these other places, but actually people were at their homes there. The units were not formed in the sense that people were stationed there. These were all people who were actually staying in their homes, and then when the battalion would be mobilised, then they would assemble in Dabar or Lusci Palanka or other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. I understand. Can you please look at document 28 that is in your binder. First we were looking at document 29, now we are going to look at 28.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yeah, just for the record, this is -- I think it's 00507489. This is ERN number. And something was mentioned there, maybe it's 65 ter list, I don't know. It's 1682.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, do you have this document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was signed by Colonel Anicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, we talked about that this morning. Let us just see whether we have that this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We are just looking for this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we are waiting for the document, I would just like to ask you a couple of things. Look at the first page of this order. As we can see this was a combat assignment involving disarming action.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Anicic named it like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Wait, wait, please, wait, please. Colonel, to speed things up, we don't have much time. We've heard your explanation. All I'm asking you now is whether it says here, and you can answer with a yes or a no, that it's a combat action of disarming in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We'll continue. In paragraph 1, does it state that the Green Berets joined the population from some neighbourhoods in the municipality of Sanski Most? Does it say that or not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have that information at hand. No one provided it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Colonel, Colonel, Colonel, please excuse me just one moment. It wasn't a state of war, you did not have that available, you don't know what was going on. We've already heard that during your testimony. Please, can you answer with a yes or no. I completely understand you. In item 1, I'm asking you, does it state that according to certain information forces of the Green Berets linked up, and this is something that you confirmed to me today, Golaja and Mahala again, does it state that in Article 1 or not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the town itself --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, I'm interrupting you. Does it state that in Article 1, please? Does it say that or not? Just tell me that.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partially, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And below that does it say that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not have that information available, and I cannot really answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Does it state in paragraph 3 on page 2 that a combat action along the Skucani Vakuf, Kamengradska Dolina, Sanski Most, Vrhpolje was underway? Does it say that there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it wasn't actually like that, the way it is stated here, because the 6th Brigade did not carry out any activities along that axis.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you, thank you, thank you. Let us continue, please. Just answer with a yes or no. Thank you, thank you, let us continue. In paragraph 4 Anicic decides to carry out artillery preparations and in co-ordination with units… to disarm the settlements of Mahala, Muhici and so on. Is that what paragraph 4 says, yes or no, please?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what paragraph 4 says; it is just that I do not know what…

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: … remit he had.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, thank you, the court will establish that. [In English] So I like to tender this document because he confirmed in my previous line of questioning all these particular details, and this document should be tendered in spite of his efforts to avoid authenticity and stuff like that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter's note that the counsel's last question and witness's answer had not been interpreted because they were too fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I understand that it's already a Prosecution exhibit, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you so much. That was my mistake then in my -- yeah, could we just have a number of this exhibit, please, from Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It was Exhibit P60.7.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, my good Colonel, let us go to document number 19 in this book of yours that you have in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: ERN number is 00946534, and this is in e-court 2D07-0022.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you have the order of the 6th Partisan Brigade in front of you, Comrade Colonel?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, dated the 18th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We are going fast and efficiently, just as we have up to date. Thus, was this order sent to the command of the 11th Battalion, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And does it state in the preamble of the order that the extremist Muslim population was getting ready for fighting against the Serbian people, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Does it go on to say that secret groups of extremists were pulling back into the woods and making dugouts there, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Does not it state in paragraph 1 of the order that the 6th Partisan Brigade will deploy along the line of Milosevici village, Grujici village, Topici village, Manjanovici [phoen] village, Kantari, Koprivna, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Does it state that armed enemy groups would be destroyed with surprise or sudden fire?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Does it not state that the civilian population would be assembled and transported to other locations?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that they would be taken out of the combat zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Does it not say that the military police would prevent all robberies and will organise monitoring of movements of personnel and vehicles, does it state that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the area where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Does it state in paragraph three that robbed articles and vehicles will be seized by the military police and taken to Lusci Palanka; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That's where the command of your brigade was, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And what happened to those vehicles and property when they were transferred to your brigade? What was the procedure? What did you do after that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look, there was an attack organised from Prijedor to Kurjevo [phoen] and that area of the woods because it was discovered that there were some large extremist groups of Muslims, and we encircled the direction towards Sanski Most to prevent them from transferring to Sanski Most. We did not go in --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you very much. Thank you. And on the second page of this document, there is a stamp of the military post of your brigade and your signature. You confirm that, do you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Would Madam Registrar be so kind, and Your Honour, with your permission, could we have exhibit number for this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 2D17, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Colonel, in this case -- first of all, do you know Mirzet Karabeg from Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In your opinion he is a straightforward person, capable of speaking the truth, he is not an evasive kind of man?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I really didn't know him that well. When I came to that area, he seemed quite temperate. I didn't have the chance to really see anything out of the ordinary with him, that he was an extremist or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you know when you were in Sanski Most in 1992 you told us about victims in your unit, but do you have any information about civilian casualties among the Serb population in that zone? Do you have any information?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no casualties in Serb villages from Muslims except in Fajtovci, where one Mirko Dosenovic had his throat cut by members of an extremist Muslim group that was going towards Bihac and they had asked them to take them across which he refused, so they slit his throat. I am not aware of any other victims while I was there, casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will finish. It's a matter of seconds. But, please, I have to locate another important document. I appreciate your understanding. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a document. Unfortunately for technical reasons I did not manage to organise to have it transferred to Belgrade, but I'm going to read so you can see what it's about. I think that you talked about it a little bit. This is ERN number [in English] 07437 and 38. [Interpretation] This is your -- well, actually it has the format of an order, just like the previous document. And it refers to the situation in the territory of the Kljuc municipality. And we're talking about --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it must be a longer ERN number than that, Mr. Pantelic. Can you just try and give us the full one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Colonel, this is an order to the command of the 10th Brigade, actually, the 10th Battalion, the 5th and the 10th Battalion where you say, I order the forces of 80 to 100 men be sent to the region of the Serbian municipality of Kljuc for the purposes of preventing conflicts. Then you say that all the deployed men should have provisions secured for the days of the 7th and 8th of May. And you sent 30 people from the 3rd Brigade, then you deployed a Special Police platoon, armoured vehicles, and so on and so forth, so all of that is a part of that order. I know that you don't have that in front of you right now, but do you recall more or less issuing such an order at one point in early May?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already spoke about the take-over of power in the municipality of Kljuc. This was when that happened, and so I drafted this order and engaged these units which prevented any conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let us confirm, then, that you know about this order, and you can see --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It also refers to a platoon for special action. What sort of a platoon is that as part of your brigade?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a platoon intended for intervention in the front if the lines were broken through. This was a crack platoon which would be closing the breaches and improving the situation at specific positions. These were selected seasoned fighters.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And was this Njunja a commander there and the rest of his men?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't Njunja. At the beginning the commander was Sveto Mrdjan, and his nickname was Crni Djordje, Black George.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, you reminded me excellently, dear Colonel, at the end. Do you remember on Sunday when we were talking about the Green Berets about this Golaja?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So what was the name, how did the Muslims, the members of that unit refer to themselves? What was the name of that unit?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Muslims that I had taken over, 146 of them into Bihac, this Captain Avdic had formed a unit there and armed it, and they were seasoned, fierce fighters, but they had called themselves the Flies of Sana.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Colonel, I have completed my cross-examination. Thank you for your cooperation and your attention, and thank you for your answers which have been recorded in the transcript here and for your interpretations of the questions. Thank you very much, and I wish you a lot of luck. I just have one more question. I would like it to be entered into the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You had been interviewed in the -- with the status of a suspect in your previous interviews with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on two occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And you said that you had some suspicions that, God forbid, perhaps you would be charged before this Sarajevo court, did you tell me something to that effect?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They have not withdrawn the charges from Sarajevo yet. They have only amended them. I'm not being tried for ethnic cleansing, genocide, and war crimes anymore, but mostly for mosques and some materiel goods.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And it was my impression when I was reading the interview that you provided to the OTP that you were quite frightened, and in those statements you seemed -- well, you often used these helping words like this, I don't know, and you were stumbling a bit. You did seem quite concerned in these years when the Prosecution had rounded you up and pressed you. Did you have the impression that that was your state of mind?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, but it also seems to me that there were a lot of mistakes in the translation and interpretation, so I was using those bywords or helping words. I was concerned because knowing what I did, this is something that I was not actually expecting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I understand. Nobody finds it easy to face them. I mean, it's not easy for us, we are waging a fierce battle here. But you had seemed quite confused and fearful during that interview in 2002; is that correct? Could you please repeat your answer, it has not been recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the first interview, I did feel frightened, and it wasn't, I wasn't really relaxed, and it wasn't all the same to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much once again, and I wish you the best of luck. Good-bye.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good-bye.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Re-examination, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Colonel, did I understand you to say you've been indicted by the state court in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had the impression that they had actually issued an indictment in The Hague against me and that I was called for my first interview on that basis. However, later when it turned out that The Hague Prosecutors did not issue charges against me, since the time I gave my first interview, I received information that there was an indictment for mosques and for some material property and so on and so forth. However, I didn't see that indictment or those charges, and I don't know much about it. This is just unconfirmed information.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So when you said they dropped some of the charges, you haven't seen anything, you are just getting information? Can you just answer that yes or no as well, please.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: From unofficial organs, I received this information.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And, of course, there's no extradition treaty between Serbia and Bosnia, is there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there isn't, but because of that information I cannot go to my birth place because I'm still afraid that I would be arrested.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Well, I want to ask you just a couple of things about -- arising from the questions you were asked. First of all, you've been shown a number of documents, and you've been referred to things that you've said about what you call the Green Berets and Muslim extremists. And in particular, you talked about a training centre in Golaja. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And your excuse for launching attacks on the various places that have been discussed is that there were -- or you had information that there were 400 or more in some places armed, what you call, Green Berets?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I said was that there were about 400 in Golaja, and I received this information, and that after the action was completed, we established that there was a centre there, that there were facilities where they were staying in where they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. And the last document that you were shown by Mr. Pantelic referred to, again, Muslim extremists and Green Berets in large numbers - and I'm not going to ask to you explain what the difference between a Muslim extremist and the Green Beret is - but do I also understand you to say that in the whole year 1992 only 123 men in the whole of your brigade were killed?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So these large numbers of allegedly armed Muslim forces in the whole of that year only managed to kill 123 of your men; is that what we are to understand? And indeed some of those men, we understand, were not actually killed in action. Is that right, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't refer to actions of the Green Beret and extremists in the Sanski Most area. These are brigade losses in other fronts, in Gradacac, the breaking through of the corridor, and so on and so forth. These are total brigade losses when I was in command.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much, Colonel, that's very helpful. So it's not just losses incurred because of actions in Sanski Most, but everywhere else that the brigade was engaged in 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Next I want to ask you about the document that you issued and you were shown on the 1st of June. I've forgotten what the exhibit number is - it's D16, is it? Thank you. Defence tab 29. Can you turn to into document again, please, Colonel. You've got it there, have you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Under item 1: "All soldiers prone to burning down and destroying buildings from which the enemy is not opening fire at the unit must be discharged." Today you told us, rather more than yesterday, that you had, as it were, persuaded Major Brajic to admit to destroying the mosque in Mahala. He made no bones about it, is what you told us today, he said he didn't need all the explosive. Was he discharged?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I forced General Talic when I was leaving to remove Major Brajic from Sanski Most and to send him to the training centre at Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'll repeat the question. "All soldiers prone to burning down and destroying buildings from which the enemy is not opening fire at the unit must be discharged." Why didn't you discharge Major Brajic there and then as a result of your own order?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't do that because he was an active officer. State of war was not proclaimed, and I had to request from my Superior Command to do that. However, the explanation I got was that he was a good senior officer, and that he should be kept.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, do you mean you did make the request to General Talic, that Major Brajic who had confessed to blowing up a mosque should be removed? And I mean in June, not in December.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't only refer to the mosque issue, but also his work and his conduct as my first assistant, and I had insisted a few times in conversations with General Talic, that he be removed from the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Did you say to General Talic, who also incidentally issued an order, didn't he, that mosques should not be destroyed or other religious documents. Did you explain to General Talic that he had confessed to blowing up a mosque and, therefore, should be dismissed?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I conveyed this to General Talic, and most probably in the end he did accept my request to remove him from the brigade because I was afraid if he did stay in the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Did you do this in June, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in June, but I did it in August and September on a number of occasions, asking him -- asking that he be re-assigned.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't want to spend too much more time on this. But why didn't you immediately when you had issued this order and Major Brajic had confessed, remove him or ask General Talic in June, not wait until August?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained that this was an active-duty officer and that I, as his brigade commander, could not do something like that. I couldn't have him removed, and General Talic couldn't do it either. This had to be done by a higher command or the personnel administration.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Let's leave that. Now, you told Mr. Pantelic a few minutes ago that after this order by you was issued on the 1st of June, no further crimes were committed in Sanski Most. Do you agree that's what you said to Mr. Pantelic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the number had gone down and that no significant crimes were committed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, that's not what you actually said, but --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is as much as I can recall for that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. On the 27th of June, did some army reservists enter the hamlet of Kenjari? Colonel?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with the date. I'm really not that good with dates, so I really couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you remember an incident, I suggest, around the 27th of June, where the inhabitants of Kenjari were ordered out, the men were separated from the women, taken towards the hamlet of Plasevici [phoen], ordered into a house, a grenade was thrown in by the soldiers and the men were killed. Do you remember an incident like that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That wasn't like that, somebody just wrote that off the top of their head. The events didn't proceed in that way, I already explained the case in Kenjari. The commander of the battalion Brajic, not Veljko Brajic, but Brajic -- not Nedeljko, Ranko. Ranko Brajic, he was the commander of the battalion, and he didn't separate the Muslim men from the women. All he did was he talked in Kenjari with those men. And they agreed to enter his battalion and that they be issued with weapons and a uniform. He left them in that house to wait until he came back from Hrustovo when the disarming of Hrustovo was complete, and then they would receive weapons and uniforms and would become members of his battalion, fighters in his battalion. However, those who killed those people actually turned up. I didn't have information about how this happened, did they throw a bomb, or exactly how they died. But I did receive information that one of those people managed to escape and the Prosecution does have that information. Those people who did that were detained. The commander of the battalion arrested those people and handed them over to the MUP in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's look at another incident, shall we. On the 1st of August, did you order the shelling of the village of Lukavica?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Selo Lukavica was never shelled, according to what I know, by the 6th Brigade. I don't have such information.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you remember an incident where 14 unarmed Muslim men were taken from the hamlet of Alibegovica?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I don't have that information. I was never advised that this was done by anyone from my brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you still want to say that no crimes were committed after you issued that order on the 1st of June?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not explain to you the time-line. I can't give you the time-line because it was a long time ago. I forgot the dates. You probably have these dates in documents right in front of you, and I must take your word for it. I must be now confused about the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And finally, I want to ask you about the two incidents where you removed people from Manjaca. You said --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I wonder if I can just have up the LiveNote. It's page 44, line 22, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You explained how you went to Manjaca and had freed someone called Captain Nijaz Halilovic. You took along a judge to Manjaca. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What was Captain Halilovic in Manjaca for?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just couldn't fathom that somebody had the idea of arresting him and taking him to Manjaca because he was of the greatest help to me in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, my question was, what was he arrested for?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because somebody had labelled him as an extremist, which he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, what does it mean to be labelled a Muslim extremist? What is the criminal offence which allows you to lock up somebody because he is a Muslim extremist?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the opposite side did the same to Serbs who were considered as extremists, and they were removed from their communities. By the same token, in this case, Mirza Kurbegovic and some others were arrested on the same charges, and they were sent to Manjaca. And Halilovic, Nijaz Halilovic, was sent the same way.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Forget what the other side may or may not have done. What is the offence which allowed the army or the police to take Captain Halilovic, who you liked, to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how people arrogate to themselves such rights. I thought it was unfair to the man. I tried to get him free, and I succeeded. As for the others, you can only ask them what they were thinking, because in my eyes, it wasn't a crime.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you have the ability to get a judge to sign a release order for this man; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I went to Banja Luka to the military court; I talked to the judge nicely. But beforehand, I had gotten files from the corps command and spoken to people there to see if they have anything specific on him. They said, No, we don't have anything firm. But still he was arrested and brought there. And I explained when I got there how much he had helped me, everything he had done, and then the military judge issued a decision and the man was released.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you managed to do the same for four other people who were -- whose parents were friends of yours; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What was the reason for their arrest?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the justification was for their arrest in Bosanska Krupa. It happened during combat operations in Bosanska Krupa, and then those able-bodied men who happened to be there were detained, in certain numbers, brought to the school and kept there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you make any other attempts it to get the files of the other hundreds and hundreds people who were in Manjaca who had been taken there from Sanski Most to have their files examined to see whether they ought to be released?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I had no time to deal with my own affairs or take care of my own family, let alone those of other people. Other bodies were in charge of that. I could not interfere because by that time the state of war had already been declared. I was not the absolute master on that territory. Everybody did their own job. The army did its own job, the MUP did theirs, and I did not want to meddle with other people's affairs, just as I did not accept anyone else meddling in mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's all I ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel, may I put a question to you here towards the end. The question is related to your repeated assertions that since a state of war had not been declared officially, there were a number of things that you could not do and indeed did not do. And I'm raising the question because you have resorted to this explanation at a number of occasions during your testimony while you have also told us that you ordered units into combat operations at several occasions, and that a number of your men were killed in combat. And you have also told us when you were shown the copy of the law of the people's defence, Article 104, that there was indeed an imminent threat of war. Now, all of this seems to me to indicate that a war had effectively broken out, and that you took part in it and did order combat operations. And yet you maintain that a state of war had not been declared, and these two points of view seem to me to be contradictory. Now, could you explain to me the reason why you have so persistently maintained that there was not a state of war?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would have to take some time to explain. Article 104 of the Law on All People's Defence, the law that had been enacted in the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia when it was expected that any aggression on our country would be from outside. In other words, at that time nobody could imagine that one day we would be waging a war of this kind with no rules at all. In this war, the rules from the Law on All People's Defence did not apply, so that we commanders, since no state of war had been declared and no marshal laws were given to us to enable us to take more effective measures, I as a brigade commander wanted to establish a marshal court which had unlimited ability to sanction and punish any perpetrators of crimes on the spot, and even execute them by firing squad. A commander with such laws in hand, could be quite energetic and put an end to all crimes, murders, and looting. However, since no state of law -- war had been proclaimed, and we were at war, we commanders muddled through as best we could, the best we could on the basis of our experience. Whenever on our territory there was looting and crimes, we were not always able to prevent it. I was often asked why did I not provide security to Muslim villages. I often did secure villages, but I had to second to this assignment my best fighting men who would have the courage to defend Muslims, because soldiers often told me, Look, I'm not going to lay down my life for Muslims. However, if the state of war had been declared, he would simply have to obey my orders. If I had done that, half of my troops would be in jail, and we would have no men to do anything on the ground. So it was very difficult to secure the land and the mosques, et cetera. I did, I did provide security to some mosques, but that was not enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand your explanation. Colonel, when was, finally, a state of war declared?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was declared after Republika Srpska was bombed, and when those men were tied to pillars so that NATO couldn't bomb anymore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the date. I think the Prosecution must have that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Colonel. Mr. Pantelic, we are over the time now, so we have to adjourn.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just to pick up one issue that you mentioned in your examination to clarify with the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Colonel, you said when Judge Harhoff asked you, you actually said you had provided security to all the mosques in the area, and the record says "some mosques." Now, to keep the record straight, you provided security to all the mosques, but some of them were still destroyed; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And you provided security to other places of worship such as Catholic churches?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO BASARA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, but I don't think the Catholic church was destroyed while I was there. I don't know about later.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Colonel Basara, we thank you very much for your assistance to the Tribunal, and you are now released as a witness. And we extend best wishes for the resolution of those health issues which prevented your travelling to The Hague. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: While the witness is being escorted --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- the office in Belgrade remind -- or announce to the parties that Room 396 has been reserved for tomorrow, Wednesday, the 14th of October, from 2.00 until 4.00. Unfortunately we could not have the room for any time beyond 4.00. But we have the meeting room for two hours from 2.00 to 4.00. So we look forward to seeing you there, and the agenda for that meeting tomorrow will be the issues that have been raised in relation to admission of the documents during 92 ter witnesses or through 92 ter witnesses, and also an attempt to make a long term planning of the next months of trial on the basis of the list of witnesses that will be provided by the Prosecution, or maybe already has been provided. So we look forward to seeing you all in Room 396 tomorrow at 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And if you permit me, I owe you a response. Thirty seconds. I owe you a response on your question where certain lines of direction was during my cross-examination, what is direction of certain line? Point number 1 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, we have to take up this tomorrow when we resume the hearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: This meeting a adjourned.
